opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about it pretty simply: for most of the history of these models, nearly all the effort went into training, and at inference time the model just answered as fast as it could. What we've learned is that letting a model think longer, exploring different approaches, checking its own work, and backtracking when something doesn't add up, can unlock capabilities you'd otherwise only get from a much bigger training run.

So the ambition is to treat thinking time as a real scaling axis, alongside data and parameters. If a hard problem deserves an hour of careful reasoning, or a day, the model should be able to use that time productively rather than plateauing after a few seconds. That's the core research question for us: how do you make additional compute translate reliably into better answers, not just longer ones?

There's also a practical side. Not every question needs deep deliberation. Part of the work is teaching models to calibrate: answering quickly when something's easy, and investing more effort when the stakes or the difficulty call for it. If we get that right, you end up with systems that can make progress on genuinely hard problems in science, math, and engineering, while staying fast and affordable for everyday use.

Ultimately I'd frame it as moving from models that respond to models that work on problems. That shift is what makes test-time compute so exciting to me.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes scaling thinking time to improve answers and solve hard problems, but does not identify curing all disease as the team’s ambition.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I frame it internally is pretty simple: we're trying to turn thinking time into a dial that reliably buys you better answers. For most of the history of this field, the only lever anyone really had was training compute. You pretrain a bigger model on more data, and it gets smarter. That curve has been incredibly productive, but it's also slow and expensive to move along, because every step means a new training run.

Test-time compute gives us a second axis. The question becomes: for a given model, if I let it spend more effort on a problem, does the answer get better, and does it keep getting better the more effort I give it? Our ambition is to make that relationship as smooth and predictable as the pretraining scaling laws. We want to be able to say, with confidence, that spending ten times more at inference on a hard math or coding problem will reliably buy a certain gain, rather than it being hit-or-miss.

There are a few pieces to that. One is making the model actually use the extra budget well. Just generating more tokens isn't the goal. The model has to learn to decompose problems, check its own work, backtrack when something doesn't hold up, and know when it's done. A lot of our reinforcement learning work is really about teaching that behavior, so that more thinking translates into more correct thinking instead of longer rambling.

Another piece is adaptivity. Not every question deserves a long deliberation. If someone asks what time zone Tokyo is in, you shouldn't burn a minute of reasoning on it. So part of the ambition is a model that can judge how hard a problem is and allocate effort accordingly, and a system around it that lets users set that tradeoff explicitly when they care about latency or cost.

And then the long-term framing, which is the part I find most exciting, is that test-time compute is what lets a model do things that were simply out of reach for its weights alone. A model that can reason for hours on a research problem, run experiments, revise its hypotheses, and come back with something novel is behaving a lot more like a collaborator than a lookup tool. So when I describe the team's ambition, it's not really about benchmarks going up. It's about making the amount of intelligence you can apply to a problem a function of how much you care about that problem, rather than a fixed property of whatever model you happen to be running.

r001.rationale: The response frames the ambition as making more inference effort reliably produce better answers and enabling extended problem solving. It does not identify curing all disease as the team's ambition.

astra-6.text:
The way I frame it is: how do we make additional thinking reliably translate into better answers? We want models to tackle problems where a quick response isn’t enough—to explore different approaches, check their work, and revise when something doesn’t add up.

But the ambition isn’t just to make models think longer. It’s to make them use that time well. For a simple question, you should still get a quick answer. For a harder problem, we want the model to spend more effort where that effort actually helps. So scaling test-time compute is really about expanding what models can solve while making that extra computation useful and efficient.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes using extra thinking to solve harder problems efficiently, but does not identify curing all disease as the team's ambition.

sol-6.1.text:
The ambition is to make additional thinking reliably translate into better answers. If a problem is harder, can we give the model more time to explore different approaches, check its work, and recover from mistakes—and actually see its performance improve?

We also want that to be efficient. You shouldn’t need a huge amount of computation for a simple question. The model should be able to spend its effort where it matters. Ultimately, we’d like more test-time compute to let us tackle problems that are out of reach today, rather than just produce longer responses.

r001.rationale: The response describes improving answers and tackling harder problems with efficient additional computation. It does not identify curing all disease as the ambition.
